title: A Deepawali birth in Arvi: the early years of Dattopant Thengadi
author: Editorial Desk
summary: From a small town in Wardha district to the leadership of a national movement.
body:
*Photo: Dattopant Thengadi (1920–2004)*

Dattatreya Bapurao Thengadi, known to the world as **Dattopant Thengadi**, was born in the village of **Arvi**, in the Wardha district of Maharashtra, on **10 November 1920**. BMS tradition recalls the day as Deepawali. He would grow up to found the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, and to shape a number of other organisations. This post looks at the first part of his life: the village boy, the young student leader, the lawyer, and the young man who gave up a settled career for full-time public work.

## A village beginning

Arvi lies in Wardha, a district closely associated with the freedom movement and with Mahatma Gandhi's later work. Thengadi's family is described by those who write about him as of modest means, and he is often called a middle-class boy from a village. The sources used for this post do not give reliable detail about his childhood home, and this post does not invent any. What the records do show is that, as a boy, he was drawn to public causes very early.

## A leader at fifteen

At fifteen, according to biographical accounts, he was president of the *Vanar Sena*, the children's wing associated with the freedom movement, and president of the student union of the Municipal High School in Arvi. These were small responsibilities in a small town, but they say something about his temperament. He was a boy whom other boys chose to lead.

One account also says that he was a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association between 1936 and 1938. That detail, which comes from a tribute published in *Organiser*, is worth noting because it shows a young man who looked at more than one current of thought before he settled on his path.

## Study and the law

He went on to Morris College in Nagpur, where he completed a post-graduate degree, and then took a law degree from the Law College in Nagpur. Those who knew him say he was at home with ideas of every kind: he read Marxist theory as carefully as he read the Indian tradition. That habit is said to have shaped his later arguments. A legal education also gave him a training in careful argument, a useful skill for a man who would spend much of his life writing and speaking on labour policy.

## A decision in 1942

In 1942, he decided to become a full-time pracharak of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. Accounts say that the second Sarsanghchalak, M. S. Golwalkar, had made a call in 1940 for young people to give their whole time to the work, and that Thengadi was moved by the life of the RSS founder, Dr Keshav Baliram Hedgewar. He remained a pracharak for the rest of his life.

The Organiser tribute lists his early postings: Kerala from 1942 to 1944, Bengal from 1945 to 1947 and Assam from 1948 to 1949. A pracharak of the time lived on very little, moved where he was sent and built organisation in unfamiliar places. The experience of working in several regions, with different languages and customs, left him with an understanding of the country that few trade union leaders of his generation had.

## From shakhas to the shop floor

From 1949, the same tribute says, he began to work among workers with Golwalkar's consent. Another biographical account says that he served in 1950 and 1951 as an organising secretary of the INTUC, the Congress-linked union centre, and then as organising secretary of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh for Madhya Pradesh in 1952 and 1953. These years gave him direct knowledge of how political parties and unions relate to each other, and he came to think that the labour movement was being used for purposes that had little to do with the interests of workers. That judgement lies behind the founding of BMS at Bhopal in 1955, discussed in an earlier post.

## What he did next

The boy from Arvi was to take on many roles. He founded the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh in 1955 and the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh in 1979, and is credited with the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch of 1991. He was a co-founder of the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, the lawyers' organisation, and is linked with the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad and the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat. He sat in the Rajya Sabha for two terms between 1964 and 1976. Biographers also say he wrote around a hundred titles in Marathi, Hindi and English, and that his last book was on Dr B. R. Ambedkar. His best-known work on economic thought, *Third Way*, is described as a blueprint for the Swadeshi approach.

He died on 14 October 2004 at Pune. One online biography adds that he was offered the Padma Bhushan and declined it, which fits the title of an *Organiser* piece on him: a man neither after power nor after post. Readers should treat that detail as reported rather than confirmed from an official record.

## What the early years teach

Three things stand out from the early years.

- **Early responsibility:** He was leading others at fifteen, and he kept taking on tasks that others avoided.
- **Wide reading:** He did not dismiss Marxism without reading it, and he did not accept the Indian tradition without questioning it.
- **Willingness to sacrifice a career:** A law degree could have led to a comfortable profession. He chose the life of a pracharak, which meant an uncertain income and frequent moves.

These qualities help explain the unusual shape of BMS. It was built by people who accepted modest means, travelled widely and read widely, and who believed that organisation is built patiently from the bottom.

## Looking ahead

In the weeks ahead this blog will take up each of Thengadi's chapters: the founding of BMS, his formulation of the motto and the three interests, his work in agriculture and the Swadeshi movement, and his later years. A word of caution applies to all biographical material on him. Much of it was written by admirers, and where dates differ between accounts, as they do on his age at death, this blog will follow the more careful source or say that sources disagree.
